Preface

This Report on the audit of expenditure incurred by the Government of West
Bengal has been prepared for submission to the Governor under Article 151 of
the Constitution. The Report covers significant matters arising out of the
compliance and performance audits of various departments including
autonomous bodies. Audit observations on the Annual Accounts of the
Government would form part of a Report on State Finances, which is being
presented separately. The Report containing the observations arising out of
audit of statutory Corporations and Government Companies and the Report
containing observations on audit of revenue receipts of the Government are
also presented separately.

The Report starts with an introductory Chapter outlining the profile of audited
entities, audit mandate, planning and extent of audit, the status of fiscal
operation of the Government of West Bengal and the key audit findings which
emerged during the year-long audit exercise. Chapter 2 of the Report covers
performance audits while Chapter 3 discusses material findings emerging from
compliance audits. Chapter 4 includes the findings arising out of the Chief
Controlling Officer based audit of Water Resources Investigation and
Development Department.

The cases mentioned in this Report are among those which came to notice in
the course of test audit of accounts during the year 2010-11 as well as those
which had come to notice in earlier years but could not be dealt with in
previous Reports; matters relating to the period subsequent to 2010-11 have
also been included wherever necessary.



Chapter 1: Introduction

1.1 About this Report

This Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (C&AG) relates
to matters arising from performance audit of selected programmes/ activities
and Government organisations and compliance audit of Government
Departments and autonomous bodies.

Compliance audit refers to examination of transactions relating to expenditure,
receipts, assets and liabilities of the audited entities to ascertain whether the
provisions of Constitution of India, applicable laws, rules, regulations and
various orders and instructions issued by competent authorities are being
complied with. On the other hand, performance audit examines whether the
objectives of the programme/activity/department are achieved economically
and effectively.

District-centric audit assesses the status and impact of implementation of
various socio-economic developmental activities in the district and evaluates
improvement in the quality of life of the people.

The primary purpose of this Report is to bring to the notice of the Legislature,
important results of audit. Auditing Standards require that the materiality level
for reporting should be commensurate with the nature, volume and magnitude
of transactions. The findings of audit are expected to enable the Executive to
take corrective actions as also to frame policies and directives that will lead to
improved financial management of the organisations, thus, contributing to
better governance.

Chapter 1, in addition to explaining the authority, planning and extent of audit,
provides a synopsis of significant audit observations, a brief analysis of the
expenditure of the Government for the last three years, budget and expenditure
controls of the Government, response of Government to draft paras/reviews
and follow up action on Audit Reports. Chapter 2 of this Report contains audit
of selected programmes/Government organisations. Chapter 3 contains
observations on compliance audit of various departments and _ their
functionaries. The findings of Chief Controlling Officer based audit of Water
Resources Investigation and Development Department have been highlighted
in Chapter 4 of the Report.

1.5 Planning and Conduct of Audit

Compliance audit is conducted as per the annual audit plan. The units are
selected on the basis of risk assessment. Audits taken up are selected on the
basis of topicality, financial significance, social relevance, internal control
system of the units, occurrence of defalcation/misappropriation/embezzlement
as well as findings of previous Audit Reports. Apart from the above
parameters, all departmental, important directorates and district level units are
audited annually so that fund flow to their subordinate formations comes to the
notice of Audit.

Inspection Reports are issued to the heads of units after completion of audit.
Based on replies received, audit observations are either settled or further
action for compliance is advised. Important audit findings are processed
further as draft paragraphs for inclusion in the Audit Report of C&AG.

In case of Performance Audit and CCO based Audit, objectives and criteria
are framed and discussed in entry conferences with the concerned
organisation. After conducting audit, the draft report is issued to the concerned
Department. Observations arising out of audit effort are also discussed with
the Departmental heads in exit conference.

Formal replies furnished by the Department as well as views expressed by the
Heads of Departments in exit conferences are carefully considered while
finalising the material for inclusion in the Audit Report. Audit Reports are laid
before the State Legislature under Article 151 of the Constitution of India.

(0) District-centric Audit of Dakshin Dinajpur

In recognition of the importance accorded by the Planning Commission,
Government of India, for a district-centric approach to devolution of finances
towards integrated local area development, a district-centric audit of Dakshin
Dinajpur District was carried out to assess the status and impact of
implementation of various socio-economic developmental activities in the
District during 2006-2011 and to evaluate improvement in the quality of life of
the people. The review covered key Social Sector programmes relating to
health, education and housing, water supply and Economic Sector
programmes relating to creation of roads, infrastructure development,
employment generation, electrification of villages.

While audit observed some positive trends in the health and education, there
are quite a few arcas that have been flagged for focused attention of the
State/District administration.

>» An area that calls for attention is the planning process to assess the gaps in
various developmental and social security programmes and develop
appropriate perspective and annual plans to bridge these gaps with proper
prioritisation and clear timelines. Audit observed that the District Plan was
either not prepared or prepared late. The State Government should build
capacity at the local level to enable the blocks to formulate plans to
address the locally felt needs.

Implementation of National Rural Health Mission (NRHM), the flagship
scheme in Health Sector, resulted in some positive impact as reflected in
increased institutional deliveries and reduced infant mortality rate.
However, Audit observed that households and facility surveys were not
conducted, perspective plan was not prepared and functioning of Rogi
Kalyan Samitis was deficient thereby compromising the idea of
community participation and ownership. No new health centres were set
up despite acute shortages and there were deficiencies in inpatient
services, operation theatres, labour room, pathological test facility etc.
Besides, there were significant shortages of medical officers and
paramedics.

In Education Sector, review of the Sarva Siksha Mission (SSA) revealed
that there was no increase in the number of elementary schools during the
last five years. Existing schools lacked requisite infrastructure like
stipulated number of class rooms, toilets, etc. as various interventions of
the Scheme were either not implemented or inadequately implemented.
Disparities in posting of teachers in the district and inadequate capacity
building of teachers may potentially affect the quality of teaching. Though
drop-out and promotion rate of students improved, enrolment of children
decreased during last five years.

In Nutrition Sector, the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS)
programme failed to provide requisite nutrition to the targeted population
for 300 days in a year mainly due to shortage in supply of food. The
Anganwadi (AW) Centres suffered from inadequate infrastructural
facilities. There were shortages of Child Development Project Officers,
which also impacted supervision of AW Centres.

> Under Water Supply, review of the implementation of the Accelerated

> In Roads Sector, though length of road increased by 73 per cent and

> Employment generation schemes like Swarna Jayanti Gram Swarozgar

from lax supervision. Under SGSY, only 16 per cent of the Self Help

March 2011. Only 36 percent of the job card holders were provided
employment on an average under NREGS, but a negligible number of
households were provided 100 days guaranteed employment.

> In Energy Sector, though the RGGVY succeeded in bringing electricity to
all the mouzas in the District, all rural households in the District could not
be energised after five years of launching the programme.

(ii) Working of Siliguri Jalpaiguri Development Authority

Located at the narrow corridor linking North-Eastern States to the rest of the
country and on the traditional trade route to Sikkim, Nepal, Bhutan and
mandated with the responsibilities of planned and integrated development of
Siliguri Jalpaiguri Planning Area (SJPA), Siliguri Jalpaiguri Development
Authority (SJDA) was constituted in April 1980. Since then, it has taken
leadership in providing connectivity with the existing state and national
highways by way of constructing new and alternative bye roads, fly-overs and
bridges and has executed a number of projects for development of housing and
transport infrastructure. Audit has flagged certain areas of concern as regards
planned use of land, strengthening financial and operational controls,
acquisition, utilisation of land, infrastructure development and internal control.

> Contrary to its statutory responsibility to prepare Land Use and
Development Control Plan within two years of notification, SIDA did not
do so in respect of substantial part of its notified area after seven to 31
years of notifications. As a result, individual development works taken up
by SJDA did not have desired linkage with long term development plans.

(iii) Chief Controlling Officer based Audit of Water Resources
Investigation and Development Department

Water Resources Investigation and Development Department (WRIDD) of the
Government of West Bengal is responsible for planning, conservation,
development, utilisation and management of water resources in sustainable
manner for both the surface and groundwater in the Minor Irrigation (MI)
sector. The Department plays a pivotal role in ensuring assured irrigation for
agriculture by bringing more and more cultivable land under assured irrigation
with minimum time and investment. The Chief Controlling Officer based audit
of WRIDD was conducted to assess the performance of the Department during
the period 2006-11. Audit observed some areas of concern relating to
institutional, compliance and programme implementation, which affected the
performance of the Department and call for Government attention.

> With a view to reduce excessive stress on ground water the 11" Five Year

Plan envisaged special emphasis on utilisation of surface water for creation
of MI potential. The Department, however, continued to depend more on
ground water for creation of Irrigation Potential (IP) in disregard to the
plan proposal.

Vacancies in key posts and inadequate infrastructure of the State Water
Investigation Directorate (SWID) adversely affected implementation of
West Bengal Ground Water Resources Act, 2005. The laboratories were
not properly equipped to analyse the chemical parameters effectively due
to non-availability of modern instruments, non-functional equipment and
irregular supply of chemicals/testing kits. None of the laboratories was
equipped for testing of heavy metals, inorganic and organic pesticides,
virological and bacteriological analysis of water samples.

> Internal control mechanism of the Department was found deficient. There
was no departmental manual for guidance of the officers and staff in
carrying out their duties and for exercising internal control over the
activities of the Department.

> During 2006-11, 11990 MI schemes having command area of 1.08 lakh ha
were handed over to unregistered beneficiary committees. Despite huge
investment in these schemes the Department did not put an effective
mechanism in place for maintenance and monitoring of the schemes to
ensure optimum utilisation of created potential.

Vv

Deficiencies in procurement, storage and accounting of materials were
noticed. Material was procured in excess of requirement which resulted in
piling of surplus materials for years.

> Utilisation of irrigation potential of Government operated MI schemes
ranged between 29 per cent and 37 per cent during the period 2006-10 due
to defunct schemes, reduction of designed command areas by habitation,
insufficient maintenance and irregular power supply. The Department did
not take effective step to revitalise the defunct schemes.

Lack of seriousness in implementation of the Act was evident as permits were
not obtained from SWID prior to installation of 3705 groundwater based MI
schemes by Water Resources Development Directorate (WRDD). Workshops
on mass awareness were conducted only in eight districts during the first five
years of implementation of the Act.

2.1 _District-centric audit of Dakshin Dinajpur

Executive Summary

In recognition of the importance accorded by the Planning Commission,
Government of India, for a district-centric approach to devolution of finances
towards integrated local area development, a district-centric audit of Dakshin
Dinajpur District was carried out to assess the status and impact of
implementation of various socio-economic developmental activities in the
District during 2006-2011 and to evaluate improvement in the quality of life of
the people. The review covered key Social Sector programmes relating to
health, education and housing, water supply and Economic Sector
programmes relating to creation of roads, infrastructure development,
employment generation, electrification of villages.

While audit observed some positive trends in the health and education, there

are quite a few areas that have been flagged for focused attention of the

State/District administration.

> An area that requires attention is strengthening the planning process to
assess the gaps in various developmental and social security programmes
and develop appropriate perspective and annual plans to bridge these gaps
with proper prioritisation and clear timelines. Audit observed that the
District Plan was either not prepared or prepared late. The State
Government should build capacity at the local level to enable the blocks to
formulate plans to address the felt needs at the grass root level.

> Implementation of National Rural Health Mission, the flagship scheme in
Health Sector, resulted in some positive impact as reflected in increased
institutional deliveries and reduced infant mortality rate. However, Audit
observed that households and facility surveys were not conducted,
perspective plan was not prepared and functioning of Rogi Kalyan Samitis
was deficient. No new health centres were set up despite acute shortages
and there were deficiencies in inpatient services, operation theatres, labour
room, pathological test facility etc. Besides, there were significant
shortages of medical officers and paramedics.

> In Education Sector, review of the Sarva Siksha Mission revealed that
there was no increase in the number of elementary schools during the last
five years. Existing schools lacked requisite infrastructure like stipulated
number of class rooms, toilets, etc. as various interventions of the Scheme
were either not implemented or inadequately implemented. There were
disparities in posting of teachers in the district. Capacity building of
teachers was also inadequate. Though drop-out and promotion rate of
students improved, enrolment of children decreased during last five years.

> In Nutrition Sector, the ICDS programme failed to provide requisite
nutrition to the targeted population for 300 days in a year mainly due to
shortage in supply of food. The Anganwadi (AW) centres suffered from
inadequate infrastructural facilities. There were shortages of CDPOs,
which also impacted supervision of AW centres.

> Under Water Supply, review of the implementation of the Accelerated
Rural Water Supply Programme in the District showed that safe drinking

> In Roads Sector, though length of road increased by 73 per cent and

2.1.1. Introduction

2.1.1.1 District profile

District Dakshin Dinajpur was created in 1992 consequent upon the
bifurcation of erstwhile West Dinajpur District. It is bounded by Uttar
Dinajpur District in the North-West, Malda District in the South-West and has
international border with Bangladesh in the North-East and South-East.

The District spans an area of 2162 sq km and is headquartered at Balurghat.
The District accounts for about 1.87 per cent (15.03 lakh) of the population of
the State (801.76 lakh) with 86.89 per cent of them residing in rural areas. The
literacy rate in the District is 64.46 per cent as against 58.83 per cent at State
level and the National average of 65 per cent. Out of 4.32 lakh families of the
district, 44 per cent (1.92 lakh families) live below the poverty line (BPL)
which matches the percentage at the State level.

NRHM aimed at providing adequate skilled manpower at all health centres as
per IPHS norms. It was seen that shortfall in manpower in test checked BPHCs,

was 61 per cent shortfall of MOs in the test checked BPHCs; while shortfalls in

(a) Accredited Social Health Activist: Under NRHM, a trained female
community health worker called Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) was
to be provided in each village in the ratio of one per 1000 population. ASHA
was to be an interface between the community and the public health system.
ASHAs were required to be provided with drug kits containing medicines for
minor ailments, oral re-hydration solution (ORS), contraceptives, etc.

Against requirement of 1460 ASHAs in the District, 1067 were selected (during
2006-11), of which 978 were trained. Though they were appointed during
April 2007 to March 2010, drug kits were supplied late to 923 ASHAs during
January 2010 to March 2011, adversely impacting their utility.

2151.9 Monitoring

In order to address the lack of oversight, being an important reasons for steady
decline of NRHM activities in the State, the Department introduced (June
2007) a system of regular periodical supervision of Government health
facilities through inspections of health centres (by officers at various levels)
and submission of monthly reports to the H&FW Department. For this
purpose, the CMOH was required to nominate officers of the district as Nodal
Officer for regular supervisions of sub-centres, BPHCs, PHCs and Rural
Hospitals of particular block. Further, physical checking of at least five per
cent of all JSY beneficiaries in the district by the District Nodal Officer is
mandatory. Scrutiny of the records of DHFWS and selected BHFWS showed
that neither the CMOH did nominate any Nodal Officer, nor was any such
monitoring done at the District level. Moreover, from records of the CMOH it
was observed that the District authorities were unaware of the order on
physical checking of JSY beneficiaries.

Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana (RGGVY) was launched by Gol

five years. The scheme is implemented with 90 per cent subsidy from Gol.
Electrification of below poverty line (BPL) rural households is fully financed
by Gol. The West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Limited
(WBSEDCL) is the implementing agency. During 2006-11, out of the

2.1.7 Monitoring

[2.4.7.1 Supervision

Guidelines for implementation of the Central and State plan schemes stipulate
monitoring requirements. However, the DM is responsible for monitoring the
overall progress of implementation of various developmental programmes and
ensuring that these are executed within the specified timeframe and approved
budget. In view of convergence of multiplicity of developmental schemes and
involvement of larger number of implementing agencies, stronger and
comprehensive district level monitoring mechanism needs to be in place.
However, in the absence of any such consolidated monitoring mechanism at
the district level, sufficiency of monitoring was not assessable against
standards set. However, that DPC convened only four review meetings during
2006-11, no meeting having been convened in 2007-08 and 2010-11, speaks
of the gaps in monitoring. Lack of monitoring impacted execution of schemes
significantly, as discussed in specific cases.

2.1.8 Conclusion

While audit observed some positive trends in the Social Sector programmes
relating to health and education, there are quite a few areas that have been
flagged for focused attention of the State/District administration.

The overall impact of various socio-economic developmental programmes
being implemented in Dakshin Dinajpur District on the living standards of the
people of the District was limited as indicated by non-achievement of targets.
The district either failed to formulate district plans or formulated these with
such delay that the exercise proved to be futile. The individual planning of
major schemes reviewed were also deficient. While PRIs are empowered to
prepare specific plans for integrated development of their area, lack of
structured annual action plans at these levels resulted in their inability to
expend funds provided to them for implementation of various programmes.
Absence of adequate participation from PRIs in the planning process is
hindering the planned progress of the District and the felt needs at the grass
root level remain unaddressed.

Under the Health sector, though Implementation of NRHM brought about
some positive effect in terms of wider coverage of institutional deliveries and
reduction in infant mortality, there is much scope for improvement as regards
setting up of new health centres and supplementing deficient facilities in
inpatient services like, operation theatres, labour room, pathological test
facility etc. Besides, significant shortages of medical officers and paramedics
were also a matter of concern, which potentially affected quality of health care
services. Functioning of Rogi Kalyan Samitis needs to be honed up for
ensuring better community participation and ownership in health delivery
services.

There was no increase in the number of elementary schools during the last five
years. Even the existing schools lacked requisite infrastructure like stipulated
number of class rooms, toilets, etc. as various interventions of the Scheme
were either not implemented or inadequately implemented. Disparities in
posting of teachers coupled with deficiencies in capacity building of teachers
might potentially affect the quality of teaching. Though drop-out and
promotion rate of students improved, enrollment of children decreased during
last five years.

ICDS programme failed to provide requisite nutrition to the targeted
population for 300 days in a year mainly due to shortage in supply of food.
Besides, not only the Anganwadi Centres (AW centres) suffered from
inadequate infrastructural facilities, supervision on their functioning was also
compromised owing to shortages of CDPOs.

Under Water supply sector, out of 24 works taken up under ARWSP during
2006-2011, two schemes due for completion in December 2010, were yet to be
completed as of July 2011, while two other schemes had not been taken up
due to land dispute and insufficiency of water sources. Slow implementation
of work resulted in safe drinking water not being supplied to school children
in quality affected area and 8.83 lakh people of fluoride affected areas. In
violation of CE’s order, Bacteriological test of the existing 40 PWSSs was not
conducted at all since July 2009. Remaining two schemes were ongoing as of
July 2011.

Even after implementation of PMGSY for last ten years, 52 per cent of the
habitations remained unconnected, though length of road increased by 73 per
cent and number of connected habitations by 64 per cent.

The components of JNNURM like sanitation and construction of houses were
restricted due to irregular supply of building material and encroachment of
land.

Employment generation schemes like SGSY and NREGS failed to make the
desired impact in the District and suffered from lax supervision. Concerted
efforts need to be taken to exercise effective oversight in order to achieve the
targets.

Though the RGGVY succeeded in bringing electricity to all the mouzas in the
District, all rural households in the District could not be energised after five
years of launching the programme.

The State Government will have to address these serious issues in order to
ensure development of Dakshin Dinajpur District at the desired pace.

Executive Summary

Located at the narrow corridor linking North-Eastern States to the rest of the
country and on the traditional trade route to Sikkim, Nepal, Bhutan and mandated
with the responsibilities of planned and integrated development of Siliguri
Jalpaiguri Planning Area (SJPA), Siliguri Jalpaiguri Development Authority
(SIDA) was constituted in April 1980 under the West Bengal Town and Country
(Planning and Development) Act, 1979. Since then, it has taken leadership in
providing connectivity with the existing state and national highways by way of
constructing new and alternative bye-roads, fly-overs and bridges and has
executed a number of projects for development of housing and transport
infrastructure. During 2006-11, 481 developmental works valuing % 256 crore
were undertaken by SJDA, of which 177 were completed up to March 2011. It has
a total notified planning area of 5.75 lakh acres under its jurisdiction and prepared
long term Master plan for land use in the form of Land Use and Development
Control Plan (LUDCP) for 1.35 lakh acres. Audit has flagged certain areas of
concern as regards planned use of land, strengthening financial and operational
controls, acquisition, utilisation of land, infrastructure development and internal
control.

> Contrary to its statutory responsibility to prepare Land Use and Development
Control Plan within two years of notification, SIDA did not do so in respect of
substantial part of its notified area after seven to 31 years of notifications. As
a result, individual development works taken up by SJDA did not have desired
linkage with long term development plans.

>» Budget management was flawed as would be evident from instances of delays
in sending budget proposals to Government and wide variation between
budget and actuals. Financial management was deficient leading to shortfall in
collection of toll charges, rents, etc. and retention of heavy cash balances in
savings and current bank accounts.

> Inability to protect its interest was apparent from the instances of

> In the absence of comprehensive policy for fixation of prices for leasing out of
land, decisions taken by SJDA were often arbitrary resulting in loss of

2.2.1 Introduction

Siliguri Jalpaiguri Development Authority (SJDA) was constituted in April 1980
under the West Bengal Town and Country (Planning and Development) Act, 1979

of Siliguri Jalpaiguri Planning Area (SJPA) by providing facilities like land,
roads, drainage system, housing complexes, industrial estates, marketing

The Annual accounts of SJDA are prepared through Chartered Accountants, while
audit of the accounts is entrusted under Section 20 (1) of CAG’s DPC Act 1971 to
the Comptroller and Auditor General of India by the Government in pursuance of

2.2.2 Organisational set up

The SJDA functions under the administrative control of Urban Development
Department and its activities are managed by a Board! constituted by the GoWB
under Section 11 of the Act, ibid. The Chief Executive Officer (CEO), who is the
Member-Secretary of the Board, supervises day-to-day activities of SIDA. There
are four wings in SJDA. They are Engineering, Planning, Administrative and
Accounts headed by Superintending Engineer, Associate Planner, Assistant
Executive Officer and Accounts Officer respectively, who assist the CEO in their
respective fields. Besides, there are 65 regular officers/staff of different cadres
and 11 personnel under contract service.

The Board of Directors of SJDA is chaired by the Minister in Charge of UD
Department with Principal Secretary of UD Department, Divisional
Commissioner of Jalpaiguri Division, District Magistrates of Darjeeling and
Jalpaiguri as Members. As per the Act, soon after the close of a year, SJDA shall
prepare a report of its activities during the preceding year and submit it to the

2.2.11 Internal Control

Internal Control is an integral component of an organisation’s management to
provide reasonable assurance that the operations are carried out economically,
effectively and efficiently to achieve the organisational objectives.

Audit noticed the following inadequacies in internal controls:

Budgetary controls in SIDA were deficient as indicated by delays in submission
of budget and significant deviation of actuals from the budget. Retention of
substantial funds in savings bank accounts depriving SJDA of interest income of
% 0.32 crore reflects lack of financial control. Absence of controls were evident as
SJDA failed to chalk out a repayment schedule although principal loan and
interest amounting to हैं 115.43 crore was overdue for repayment to GoWB.

Further, as per PW code, any construction work, estimates of which exceeds
र₹ 1.25 crore, requires sanction of Chief Engineer (CE). Test-check, however,
showed that out of 10 such works, technical approval of three were obtained from
CE (Construction Board), PWD, while the remaining seven were approved by SE,
SJDA. The Authority stated (July 2011) that the same had to be done as SE was
the highest technical authority under SJDA. In the exit conference it was
intimated that Government received proposal for sanction of post of CE in SJDA.
Principal Secretary, however, opined that such cases should have been referred to
outside agencies with appropriate technical expertise, like Engineering College
authorities.

2.2.12 Conclusion

The objective of planning and development of SJDA was adversely affected as
SJDA, ignoring its statutory responsibility to prepare Land Use and Development
Control Plan within two years of notification, did not prepare the same in respect
of substantial part of its notified area, even after seven to 31 years of notifications.
As a result, development works undertaken by SJDA did not have the desired
linkage with long term development plan.

Budget management was flawed as would be evident from instances of delays of
29 months and 17 months in sending budget proposals to the Department.
Instances of non-initiation and abandonment of works due to non-receipt of
Budget allotments were also noticed.

Lack of internal controls over realisation of revenue led to loss on account of
unrealised toll charges, rents, etc. Retention of heavy cash balances in bank
savings and current accounts without gainfully investing them in term deposits led
to loss of possible additional interest.

Indifference towards financial interest of the Authority was also apparent from
instances of non-registration of acquisition of 462.43 acres of land, acquisition of
excess land than requisitioned by a requiring body, transfer of land in excess of
actual acquisition to a requiring body free of cost. Besides, 48.748 acres of land
acquired at हैं 7.83 crore was under encroachments

For sound financial administration and financial control it is essential that

In the course of audit of State Government Departments and their

3.2.3 Infructuous expenditure in sinking of Rig Bored Tubewells

Four Public Health Engineering Divisions sunk rig bored tube wells in the
hard rocky parts of the State without ascertaining the availability of suitable
aquifer from the concerned authorities. This led to an infructuous
expenditure of 6.37 crore.

In the hard rocky parts of the Districts of Purulia, Bankura, Birbhum and western
part of Bardhaman, ground water is accumulated in restricted and limited’?
manner due to heterogeneity in aquifer system. The Public Health Engineering
Department (PHED) is entrusted with the function of supplying safe potable water
to the people living in that part by sinking of rig bored tube wells (RBTWs).
Though aquifers in these districts were rare and scarce”’, the PHED did not assess
beforehand the availability of aquifer at the sites selected by the Zilla Parishads
for successful sinking of RBTWs.

Audit scrutiny revealed that during 2004-11 the PHE Divisions sunk 13049
RBTWs in those four districts at the sites selected by the respective Zilla
Parishads without assessing the availability of potable ground water through the
State Water Investigation Directorate (SWID), the authority competent to assess
the quality and quantity of potable ground water in the State. Consequently,
sinking of 16407 RBTWs failed due to non-availability of suitable aquifer. These
also included 137 cases of repeat borings at the same selected sites although
suitable aquifer was not available earlier. As a result, the Department incurred an
expenditure of %6.37 crore on men and material on unsuccessful boring of
RBTWs.

All the four divisional authorities accepted (April-June 2011) that the incidence of
unsuccessful sinking of RBTWs could have been avoided had the sites been
selected after obtaining technical guidance and support from the SWID.

Thus, due to failure in obtaining technical assistance from SWID to ascertain the
availability of suitable aquifer before sinking of RBTWs, the Department had to
incur an infructuous expenditure of € 6.37 crore.

The matter was referred to the Government in June 2011 but reply has not yet
been received (November 2011).

3.3.2 Lack of response of Government to audit

Principal Accountant General (Audit) (PAG) arranges to conduct periodical
inspection of Government Departments to test-check transactions and verify the
maintenance of important accounting and other records as per prescribed rules
and procedures. These inspections are followed up with Inspection Reports (IRs)
issued to the heads of offices inspected with copies to next higher authorities.

observations contained in the IRs and rectify defects and omissions promptly and
report compliance to PAG. Serious irregularities are also brought to the notice of

4.1 Introduction

Agriculture is the primary occupation in West Bengal which contributes about
20 per cent of the Net State Domestic Product. About 70 per cent of the
population are dependent on agriculture for their livelihood. Minor Irrigation
(MI) has played a pivotal role in boosting agricultural production in the State
by bringing more and more land under assured irrigation round the year. MI
schemes!, which require less investment and low maintenance cost are more
acceptable to the farmers. The ultimate gross potential of MI schemes in the
State has been assessed at 44.34 lakh hectares (ha) against 26.83 lakh ha
through Major and Medium Irrigation (MMI) Schemes’. Total Irrigation
Potential (IP) created? upto 2008-09 was 38.99 lakh ha (72 per cent) under MI
schemes against 15.76 lakh ha (28 per cent) under MMI project.

The MI Schemes from both the surface water and groundwater are executed
and operated by the Water Resources Investigation and Development
Department (WRIDD). The Department is responsible for planning,
conservation, development, utilisation and management of water resources in
sustainable manner in the MI sector. The Government introduced ‘West
Bengal Ground Water Resources Management, Control and Regulation
(WBGWR) Act, 2005’ for conservation and management of groundwater,
which is also implemented by the Department.

4.2 Organisational structure

The Department is headed by a Secretary who is the Chief Controlling Officer
(CCO). There are two Directorates viz Water Resources Development
Directorate (WRDD) and State Water Investigation Directorate (SWID), four

The function of WRDD is mainly to develop existing potential of water

The SWID carries out investigation and assessment of surface water and

The Command Area Development & Water Management (CADWM)

The primary objective of CADWM Programme was to bridge the gap between
the irrigation potential created through the canal network of the major
irrigation schemes and the area actually irrigated to make the best use of the
available land and water resources to increase agricultural production.

4.6.1 Planning

For effective implementation of the MI schemes and the WBGWR Act, 2005
the Department was required to prepare a Five year plan, which was to be
staggered into Annual Action Plans (AAPs), based on current data base of
ground water and surface water resources, achievement of creation and
operation of MI schemes already planned/taken up etc. The deficiencies
noticed in audit are discussed below:

4.6.1.1 Fourth Minor Irrigation Census Report

Rationalisation of MI statistics was launched in 1986-87 by Government of
India to build a comprehensive and reliable database of number of MI
structures created and potential utilised through these schemes. Accordingly,
an all India census of MI structures was to be conducted on quinquennial
basis.

Audit observed that the 3™ MI Census with the reference year 2000-01 was
published in December 2003. The 47" MI census (2006-07) taken up in July
2007 was scheduled to be published by June 2010. However, a draft State
level report has been prepared only in October 2011. Thus the plans (2006-11)
prepared by the Department was based on the database of 3" MI Census.

The Director, SWID stated (July 2011) that the field work was delayed due to
shortage of manpower. Validation work suffered due to discrepancy of data
and rechecking of data upto village level which took much time.

4.6.1.2 District profile and estimation of dynamic ground water resources

As per section 9 of the Act, SWID was to prepare district wise profile of
ground water resources and district plan for conservation, maintenance and
utilisation of ground water for every five year period. However, scrutiny
revealed that district profiles and district plans were not prepared for any of
the districts in the State as of October 2011 even after six years of enactment
of the Act.

As per National Water Policy, 2002, the groundwater resources should be
re-assessed periodically. Estimation of dynamic groundwater resources in
West Bengal was made in March 2004 by SWID jointly with Central Ground
Water Board (CGWB). Out of total 341 blocks in the State, ground water
assessment was made in respect of 269 blocks excluding 72 saline infested
blocks (59 in the coastal area and 13 in northern hilly region). Fresh estimation
of dynamic ground water resources in the State was made in 2008-09. The
Report of the latest estimation was not finalised as of July 2011. Lack of
comprehensive and current data adversely affected the planning and execution
of the MI schemes. Further, Section 7 (3) of the Act provided issuance of
permits for sinking of new tube wells after scrutiny of the application forms in
terms of quantity and quality of ground water. Audit noticed that due to non
availability of latest assessment data, the SWID had to follow the
categorisation of block as per estimation of ground water resources done in
March 2004 while issuing permits for sinking of new tube wells. The
possibility of over exploitation of ground water in some areas can not be ruled
out and the whole exercise of issuing permits for sinking of new tube wells
based on assessment of ground water availability was rendered infructuous.

4.6.1.4 Lack of preliminary survey and investigation in selection of schemes

Irrigation schemes were required to be taken up after carrying out detailed
survey of availability and requirement of water considering hydrological,
environmental and ecological aspects of the schemes. As per guidelines for
issue of water availability certificate for RLI schemes, SWID was required to
consider data of three years to assess the sustainability of the water sources.

The proposals of the new schemes are investigated by the departmental
engineers for preparation of the techno feasibility reports after obtaining
clearance of availability of required water from SWID. The list of feasible
schemes is submitted to District Site Selection Committee (DSSC) for
approval. Approved schemes are taken up by the Department for execution
under fund from Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF), Accelerated
Irrigation Benefit Programme (AIBP) and State Plan.

The Department took up 14,046 schemes under RIDF-VIII to RIDF-XV and
AIBP-Phase-I during 2002-10 of which 131 schemes having an estimated cost
of & 22.31 crore were dropped after approval (Appendix 4.3). Further, sites of
102 MI schemes under RIDF projects’ were subsequently changed which
resulted in delay in completion.

The Department attributed (November 2011) non-availability of suitable
aquifer, change of river courses and dried up water sources as reasons for
dropping of the schemes after approval. Scrutiny, however, revealed that
SWID considered the water availability data of a particular date against the
prevailing norms of three consecutive years before issuing water availability
certificate towards installation of RLI schemes. Thus, adequate survey and
investigations were not conducted before submission of proposals for
construction of the MI schemes.

4.7.2.2. Non-reconciliation of issue of cheques and remittances

In terms of Para 22.3.1 of Central Public Works Accounts Code, public works
divisions are required to furnish to the Accounts Office details of cheques
drawn, cheques encashed and balance of cheques remaining uncashed in
Form-51 “schedule of settlement with treasury”-Part-II, duly supported with
“Certificate of Treasury Issues” (CTIs) provided by the Treasury Officer.
Similarly, the divisions are also to furnish “schedule of settlement with
treasuries” in Form-51-Part-I, duly supported with Form-50 “Consolidated
Treasury Receipts” (CTRs) showing therein the amount remitted to the
treasuries, amount acknowledged by the treasuries and balance remaining
unacknowledged at the end of each month. It was, however, noticed that out of
24 test-checked divisions having cheque drawing power, in 14 divisions
CTIs and CTRs were in arrear for the period prior to 2006-11. As regular
reconciliation gives the opportunity of timely detection of irregularities like
missing credit, bounced cheques, misappropriation of departmental receipts,
fraudulent drawal of funds etc., absence of reconciliation leaves the scope of
such irregularities.

As per provisions of the WBGWR Rules 2006, any user desiring to sink a
tubewell is required to deposit the application fee in the treasury and submit a
copy of the treasury challan to the DLA/CLA in support of payment of
application fee. Scrutiny of records of three Geological divisions’ under
SWID revealed that there was no system of cross verification of the copy of
the treasury challan with the records of the treasury, leaving the scope of
submission of fake challans. The Secretary, WRDD in the exit conference
(November 2011) accepted the audit contention of non-reconciliation of
amount remitted to Treasury/Bank and assured to take necessary steps in this
regard.

4.7.2.3 Lapsed deposits not credited to the government account

West Bengal Treasury Rules, 2005, provides that all deposits or balances in
excess of % 25 unclaimed for more than three complete accounting years after
the year of deposit should be credited to the Government account as ‘lapsed
deposit’. In 15 test checked divisions”> of WRDD, security deposits amounting
to हैं 28.11 lakh deducted from the agencies up to March 2008 and remained
unclaimed for more than three years had not been credited to Government
account as ‘lapsed deposit’ as of March 2011, in violation of the above
provision. The Department accepted (November 2011) that the unclaimed
amount is to be deposited in the Government account as a lapsed deposit.

4.7.3__Lack of control over collection of water rates

As per National Water Policy (2002), water charges should be fixed in such a
way so that the operation and maintenance charges are covered for

checked divisions of WRDD which operated and maintained MI schemes,

cost of the schemes during the period 2006-10. Water rates for supply of
irrigation water through MI schemes under the State Government were last
revised in July 2003. Thus, the water rate fixed by the Department did not
commensurate with the actual operation and maintenance cost of the MI
schemes.

Further, realisation of water rates against supply of irrigation water from the
MI installations of WRDD are being done by the different Block Development
Officers (BDOs) in the State. The beneficiaries were to deposit water rates in
advance to the BDOs for availing irrigation facilities. On production of the
prepaid receipt issued by the BDOs, operators of the schemes record the same
in their log book and release water accordingly. Scrutiny, however, revealed
that water rates amounting to % 9.50 crore remained unrealised as of
March 2011 (Appendix 4.10). In reply, the EEs stated (March to June 2011)
that water rates were collected by the concerned BDOs and they had no
control over collection of water rates. However, the fact that the BDO
functioned as a mere collector and imposition of water rates and release of
water for irrigation after verifying paid challans were the responsibilities of
the concerned divisions of the WRDD. There was no coordination between the
divisions and BDOs in this regard. The poor collection, in comparison to the
amount due, was indicative of inadequate control and monitoring by the

4.7.5 Material and store management

A sound system of stores management involves planning of purchase
requirements, efficient and economic procurement, control over issue, timely
and proper accounting and safe physical custody of stores. Audit noticed the
following deficiencies in inventory management as discussed below:

4.7.5.1 Deficiency in accounting of stores

A large part of the estimated cost of MI Schemes is the material cost. Audit
scrutiny of 15 test checked divisions” of WRDD revealed that no Suspense Head
for ‘Stock’ was operated and expenditure incurred on procurement of material
was booked directly to the respective scheme head or maintenance head. As per
CPWA Code, material-at-site accounts for every individual work was required to
be maintained when expenditure was directly booked against the final head of
accounts. Scrutiny revealed that none of the test checked divisions maintained
material-at-site accounts. As a result, value of excess materials of a particular
scheme remained unutilised in the store and the booked expenditure of the work
remained inflated. However, store ledgers were maintained in sub-divisional
stores for keeping account of the quantity of the materials. “Bin Cards” and
“Price Store Ledger” showing quantity and value of material were also not
maintained and as such value of material available with the Department could not
be ascertained in audit.

As per Rule 244 of WBFR, material which is no longer required in the work
should be disposed off by transfer or sale. However, it was seen in audit that
proper account of surplus/unserviceable/obsolete stores were not maintained in
any of the test checked divisions. In absence of such mechanism, total value of
such stores in the Department and their disposal could not be ascertained in
audit.

4.7.5.2 Excess procurement

Rule 101 of WBFR provides that procurement of stores should be made in the
most economical manner in accordance with the requirement. Accordingly,
requirement of material is to be assessed on the basis of the detailed project
reports prepared after proper survey and investigation of individual schemes.

Funds for the procurement of material were directly provided to the Resources
Divisions*', Material procured by these divisions was to be kept in their
sub-divisional stores and should be lifted by the working divisions from those
stores as per requirement. Audit scrutiny revealed that materials worth
% 6.63 crore procured for RIDF-X to XIII between December 2005 and
November 2008 were lying unutilised (January 2011) in the sub-divisional stores
of Kolkata (A-M) Resources Division, due to non-lifting of materials by the
working divisions. The materials were not lifted as the schemes were dropped
subsequently.

4.8.3.2 Participatory Irrigation Management

MoWR (Gol) circulated (1998) a model Act to be adopted by the State

enacted in West Bengal as of November 2011. As per the guidelines of

4.8.3.3 Collection of beneficiaries’ contribution

With a view to make the water users more involved with the CADWM
programme, the Gol has decided that 10 per cent of the cost of construction of
field channels will be collected as contribution from the water users before
execution of the work and formally incorporate the same in the accounts.

Scrutiny revealed that mandatory contributions from beneficiaries were not
collected by the two test checked CAD divisions prior to execution of the
schemes. Responsibility of realisation of the contributions was passed on to
the Pradhans of the GPs through which works were executed. In the tender
agreements it was mentioned that 10 per cent of the value of the works would
be realised by the GPs from the water users. Payment limited to 90 per cent of
the work value was made to the Pradhans by the divisions and booked in the
accounts. Thus, violating the guidelines the contributions from WUAs were
not incorporated in the accounts. Moreover, in absence of any record in the
divisions it could not be ascertained whether the contributions were actually
collected from the water users.

Meanwhile, the Department recommended (November 2011) to the MoWR.
Gol to waive 10 per cent beneficiary contribution against land donated by the
farmers and manual labours.

4.9 Conclusion

The objective of development of irrigation potential and its utilisation was not
achieved to the desired extent due to inherent deficiencies in planning,
execution and monitoring. Planning was not based on updated data and targets
were fixed without any input from field offices. The Department continued to
depend more on ground water in disregard to the Eleventh Five year plan
(2007-12) proposal. Adequate survey and investigations were not carried out
before taking up of schemes. Created IP could not be utilised optimally due to
existence of defunct schemes. Utilisation of irrigation potential of handed over
schemes was not monitored. Internal control measures were not strictly
followed. Non-observance of budgetary procedure resulted in under-utilisation
of funds. There were deficiencies in procurement, storage and accounting of
materials. Implementation of WBGWR Act, 2005 by the SWID hampered due
to inadequate infrastructure as well as human resources and lack of mass
awareness. Without ensuring the sustainability of created assets and putting
effective mechanism for their maintenance, MI schemes were handed over to
unregistered beneficiary committees. Utilisation of created IP of major
irrigation projects through CADWM programme suffered due to slow progress
and non enactment of suitable Participatory Irrigation Act.

4.10 Recommendations

e The Department needs to prepare plans based on the updated data and
feedback of performance from the implementing formations and fix
realistic targets.

The Department needs to redirect its strategies to reduce excessive
dependence on ground water resources, especially in arsenic and
fluoride affected districts.

The Department should give special emphasis to revitalise the defunct
schemes for optimum utilisation of the created irrigation potential. The
Department also needs to address on the major issues like operation,
maintenance and sustainability of the handed over schemes.

SWID is to be equipped with modern equipments and infrastructure to
ensure effective implementation of the WBGWR Act, 2005.

1 Overview of State Public Sector Undertakings
Audit of Government companies is governed by
Section 619 of the Companies Act, 1956. The
accounts of Government companies are audited by
Statutory Auditors appointed by CAG. These
accounts are also subject to supplementary audit
conducted by CAG. Audit of Statutory
corporations is governed by their respective

for 2010-11 as per their latest finalised accounts.

GDP indicating an important role played by State
PSUs in the economy.

Long Term Loans) in 90 PSUs was
` 39,535.91 crore. It grew by over 15.83 per cent
from ` 34,131.73 crore in 2005-06. Power and
finance sectors accounted for nearly 80.88 per
cent of total Investment in 2010-11. The
Government contributed ` 982.83 crore towards
Equity, Loans and Grants/Subsidies during 2010-
11.
Performance of PSUs
During the year 2010-11, out of 72 working
P S U s ,3 0P S U se a r n e dP r o f i to f` 550.58 crore

Transmission Company Limited

2 Performance audit relating to Government Companies
Performance Audit relating to ‘Performance of power distribution utility in West Bengal’
in respect of West Bengal State Electrici ty Distribution Company Limited and ‘Post
restructuring performance and implementation of modernisation scheme’ by Durgapur
Chemicals Limited were conducted. Execu tive summary of audit findings of
‘Performance of power distribution utility in West Bengal’ is given below:
Electricity is an essential requirement for all
facets of our life and critical infrastructure for
country’s socio-economic development. Supply
of electricity at reasonable rate to all the sectors
is very crucial for sustained economic
development. In West Bengal, electricity
distribution is undertaken by five agencies i.e.
West Bengal State Electricity Distribution
Company Limited (Company) and The Durgapur
Projects Limited (DPL) in the State sector,
Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) in the
concurrent sector and CESC Limited and DPSC
Limited in the private sector.
As on 31 March 2011, the State had distribution
network of two lakh CKM, 549 sub-stations and
7,600.33 MVA distribution transformers (DTR)
of various categories. There were 105.72 lakh
consumers as of March 2011. The turnover of
the State distribution companies was
` 17,084.67 crore in 2010-11, which represents
3.71 per cent of State Gross Domestic Product.
These companies employed 31,430 employees as
on 31 March 2011.
Distribution network planning
The increase in Company’s distribution capacity
did not match the pace of growth in consumer
demand since connected load grew at 48 per cent
while transformer capacity increased at 27 per
cent during 2006-11. The gap of transformation
capacity to total connected load ranged between
0.63 and 0.82 resulting in frequent tripping and
adverse voltage regulation with consequential
higher quantum of energy losses.
Implementation of Centrally sponsored schemes
Under RGGVY, 3,665 villages were electrified
out of 4,283 villages taken up, while only
12.75 lakh out of 26 lakh BPL households were
provided electric connection during 2006-11.
The Company incurred extra expenditure of
` 102.08 crore in execution of works due to
placement of orders at higher rates compared to
approved estimate, inclusion of price variation
clause instead of fixed cost envisaged in the
scheme and double payment on earthing
materials. Besides, Company had to forgo
administrative charges of ` 66.08 crore as
estimates exceeded sanction limits.
Implementation of Restructured Accelerated
Power Development Reforms Programme
(RAPDRP), intended to strengthen Distribution
Management System and upgradation of sub-
transmission & distribution network, fell short of
target and the Company utilised 24 per cent of
the funds released due to delay in completing
loan formalities and slow progress of work.
Operational efficiency
The power purchases from State and Central
PSUs were not adequate to fulfill the demand in
the State and shortfall was met through purchases
from IPPs and other sources at higher rates
ranging from ` 2.49 per unit to ` 4.30 per unit.
The energy losses of 3,396 MUs valuing
` 1,311.47 crore were in excess of norms
approved by WBERC. The main reasons for
such losses were inadequate transformation
capacity, high interruption, non rationalisation of
feeders, low power factor, low feeder
availability, theft of electricity, etc. The
Company delayed in rationalising feeders that
led to non reduction of line loss of 865.24 MUs
valued ` 269.96 crore. Further, there was
significant shortfall in addition of capacitor
banks which led to loss of targeted energy saving
of 73.60 MUs valued at ` 22.96 crore. The
percentage of consumers checked was negligible
in all the years and the unrealised amounts were
on the rise.
Financial management
The Company’s Accumulated Losses decreased
by 45 per cent between 2007-08 to 2010-11 as
they had earned profit of ` 305.25 crore. In this
period, Annual Revenue Requirement petitions
were filed on time. However, the percentage of
deficit in recovery of fixed cost varied from 8 to
38 per cent during 2007-11. Besides, as of
March 2011, the Company had retained
Regulatory Assets aggregating to
` 3,320.05 crore. Agriculture was heavily
subsidised with only 31 to 50 per cent of cost of
supply being recovered. Commercial consumers
bore this burden.

Overview
(xi)
Billing efficiency
Energy billed during 2007-11 rose from 73.47 to
79.80 per cent of the total energy available for
sale. This increase was due to installation of
electronic meters which led to accurate billing.
Average billing declined from 4.42 per cent to
1.13 per cent during this period due to decline in
consumers with defective meters.
Wrong classification of commercial units as
industrial units led to loss of revenue of
` 1.20 crore to the Company. In 15 divisions
during 2008-09 to 2010-11, 21.63 lakh bills
against 5.67 lakh L&MV consumers were short
of minimum charges. Besides, average bills for
86,057 consumers with defective meters could
not be raised since previous meter readings were
not recorded.
Revenue collection efficiency
The outstanding dues from consumers decreased
from ` 1,234.81 crore in 2006-07 to ` 1,047.80
crore in 2010-11. Of the above, dues of
` 585.51 crore from 15 divisions indicated that
dues outstanding for more than three years
amounted to ` 136.37 crore (23.29 per cent)
while an amount of ` 85.20 crore (14.55 per
cent) was due from disconnected consumers.
Further, arrears of more than rupees one lakh was
due from 3,834 L&MV consumers in
15 divisions and 3,029 HT and EHT consumers
of the Company, for three to 318 months but
their supply was not disconnected resulting in
accumulation of arrears of ` 236.13 crore (March
2011).
The Company had temporarily disconnected
supply of power to 79 L&MV consumers in
15 divisions and 449 HT and EHT consumers of
the Company, having arrear of more than rupees
one lakh for four to 189 months but were not
permanently disconnected. This resulted in non-
realisation of arrears amounting to ` 22.05 crore
(March 2011). In addition, cheques of
` 3.12 crore had not been credited by the
concerned banks in six divisions but the
Company could not identify the consumers.
Consumer satisfaction
The Company created (January 2009) Customer
Relation Management (CRM) Cell to look into
the grievances of consumers and their redressal.
The Company paid ` 3.26 crore as compensation
to the consumers for non-compliance of WBERC
Regulations.
Energy Conservation
The Company is State Designated Agency
(SDA) under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001
(Act). BEE had disbursed (January 2008 to
April 2011) ` 1.95 crore to the Company for
energy conservation. The Act stipulates that the
State Government was to constitute Energy
Conservation Fund for promotion of efficient use
of energy and its conservation. The State
Government belatedly (September 2010) notified
creation of West Bengal Conservation Fund.
They were yet to contribute their share to the
fund.
Energy accounting and audit
The Company placed (October 2006/ April 2007)
orders on Secure Meters Limited (SML) for
erection of 15,230 energy accounting meters at
an extra expenditure of ` 2.43 crore towards
higher erection charges and payment of service
tax included in the rates. Further, the Company
incurred extra expenditure of ` 10.15 crore by
allowing maintenance charges on these meters
though the purchase orders provided for
maintenance of these meters free of cost for five
years.
Due to erroneous stock accounting, the Company
procured 4.42 lakh meters worth ` 40.58 crore in
excess of requirement. Besides, we could not
vouchsafe existence of 1.40 lakh meters valued
` 13.17 crore.
Conclusion and Recommendations
The Company did not prepare target for annual
capacity development of sub-stations over the
review period. The increase in distribution
capacity did not match the pace of growth in
consumer demand. They incurred extra
expenditure on execution of rural electrification
work on placement of orders at higher rates.
High energy losses were due to low feeder
availability, high interruption, voltage
fluctuation, inadequate number of shunt
capacitors and low power factor. The Company
lost opportunity to earn higher revenue due to
incorrect application of tariff, under assessment
of revenue and short levy of minimum charges.
The review contains six recommendations which
include creation of infrastructural facilities
keeping in view demand growth, reduction of
high energy losses by installing adequate number
of shunt capacitors, minimising interruptions and
voltage fluctuations. Achieving 100 per cent
energy billing, applying correct tariffs and
levying minimum applicable consumer charges
as well as optimising internal resource generation
by improving billing and collection efficiency
and vigorously pursuing outstanding dues.

Audit Report No. 4 (Commercial) for the year ended 31 March 2011
(xii)
Executive summary of audit findings of ‘Post restructuring performance and
implementation of modernisation scheme’ by Durgapur Chemicals Limited is given
below:
Durgapur Chemicals Limited (Company) was
incorporated in July 1963 with the object of
manufacturing phenol, phthalic anhydride (both
since discontinued), caustic soda, chlorine and
hydrogen with mono-chlorobenzene (MCB),
mixed dichloro benzene (DCB), sodium penta
chlorophenate (SPCP), stable bleaching powder
(SBP) and synthetic hydrochloric acid (syn-
HCL) as the primary downstream chlorinated
products by use of salt, benzene, hydrated lime
and phenol as main raw materials. The Company
played a marginal role in caustic chlorine
industry (seven per cent production) of eastern
India.
In order to turn around the Company from
incurring continuous losses due to obsolete plant
and technology, higher cost and increasing
dependence on budgetary support to meet
operational deficit, the State Government
undertook a financial cum operational
restructuring and business optimisation during
February 2004 to July 2010. The performance
audit covered the period from 2006-07 to
2010-11 to assess the post restructuring
performance of the Company.
Financial management
As a result of financial restructuring the Paid up
Capital reduced from ` 406.01 crore to
` 57.28 crore as on March 2011. For
implementation of modernisation of projects the
borrowings of the Company increased from
` 6.29 crore to ` 62.60 crore during 2006-11
registering a growth of 895 per cent .T h e
Company failed to mobilise adequate working
capital due to their inability to generate own
resources. The Company could not recover their
cost of operation as cost growth outstripped the
growth of sales realisation during 2007-11. The
poor financial health of the Company was
attributable to high cost of raw materials, power,
utility and lack of flexibility of product mix that
could fetch higher margins.
Financial, Administrative and Business
restructuring
Under capital restructuring State Government
Loan and Interest of ` 369.92 crore was first
converted into Equity and then Paid up Capital
was reduced to ` 57.28 crore as of March 2011,
by setting off the Accumulated Loss of
` 351.93 crore.
Though the Company reduced their manpower
by implementing Early Retirement Scheme they
failed to restrict their employee cost to industry
benchmark due to non implementation of
variable pay structure and thereby incurred extra
expenditure of ` 26.06 crore during 2006-11.
Delay in implementation of modernisation
project led to time overrun of 21 months and cost
overrun of ` 35.77 crore. Deviation from DPR
during implementation caused mismatch in
capacities of different up and down stream plants
and also created shortage of working capital.
Lack of proper planning and injudicious decision
making with respect to various functional
activities of the plants led to reduced production
and high costs affecting profitability of the
Company.
Production performance
Capacity utilisation of caustic chlorine plant was
71 per cent and that of MCB, DCB and SBP
plants were 34, 22 and 45 per cent during
2006-11. The production loss due to non
achievement of targets was 70,044 MT valued at
` 160.12 crore with contribution loss of
` 20.74 crore. Poor production performance was
attributed to delay/ non-completion of plant
modernisation, inadequate provision to utilise
byproducts, shortage of storage capacity and
working capital. The Company did not follow
industry norms fixed in DPR for consumption of
salt and chemicals resulting in excess
consumption of 22,992 MT of salt, benzene,
caustic soda and other chemicals over norms and
thereby incurred avoidable expenditure of
` 14.95 crore during 2006-11.
Procurement of salt
The Company procured primary raw material,
(salt) largely from a single vendor during
2006-11 at 16 to 75 per cent higher prices than
their competitors. Besides, due to poor
procurement mechanism, the Company could not
ensure capacity utilisation of the plant and ran
the risk of zero stock. Purchase through traders
instead of direct purchase from manufacturers
cost the Company avoidable expenditure of
` 5.10 crore during 2006-10.

Overview
(xiii)
Energy management
Though DPR recommended for captive power
plant for cheap source of power, the Company
did not visualise importance of power cost
sensitivity to project profitability. Power cost
ranged between ` 2.90 to ` 4.01 per unit during
2008-11 as against the envisaged cost in DPR of
` 2.25 to ` 3 and competitors’ cost at ` 2.05 to
` 2.20 per unit. Besides, the Company consumed
excess energy valued at ` 9.69 crore over the
norms during 2006-11, affecting their
profitability further. They incurred extra
expenditure of ` 7.48 crore on steam generation
due to use of costly furnace oil instead of cheaper
coal.
Sales performance
Despite high level of acceptability of the
Company’s products in the market, sales targets
were not met due to inefficiency and bottlenecks
in production. Due to faulty agreement with a
contractor, forward sale contract with a buyer
and lower realisation from sales through agents,
the Company incurred loss of revenue of
` 4.90 crore. Further, injudicious decision to
appoint commissioning agents before
commencement of enhanced production resulted
in unfruitful expenditure of ` 43.23 lakh.
Internal control
Weak internal control and monitoring
mechanism resulted in acceptance of substandard
quality of salt, lack of preventive maintenance of
the plants leading to excess down time and
resultant loss of production, lack of vigorous
pursuance of debtors resulting in bad debts and
salt being issued without recording the quantity
of salt. Further, internal audit was not effective
because neither the management took corrective
actions on shortcomings noticed in internal audit
nor did the BoD seek action taken note
thereagainst.
Conclusion and Recommendations
Restructuring plans were implemented partially
and belatedly, affecting production performance
and profitability and thereby frustrating the
objectives of revival of the Company and
breaking free from dependence on the budgetary
support of the State Government. Besides, lack
of focused sales, faulty agreements and failure to
utilise own marketing setup resulted in lower
sales realisation. The Company should explore
inexpensive and steady sources of power, rejig
their debt structure, adhere to operational norms,
procure raw materials directly from source,
introduce new value added products, increase
sale of downstream products, streamline
marketing activities by widening customer base
and strengthen control mechanism in all
operational areas.

backlog in accounts in a time bound manner.

2.1 Performance of power distribution utility in West Bengal
Executive Summary
Electricity is an essential requirement for all
facets of our life and critical infrastructure for
country’s socio-economic development. Supply
of electricity at reasonable rate to all the sectors
is very crucial for sustained economic
development. In West Bengal, electricity
distribution is undertaken by five agencies i.e.
West Bengal State Electricity Distribution
Company Limited (Company) and The
Durgapur Projects Limited (DPL) in the State
sector, Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC)in
the concurrent sector and CESC Limited and
DPSC Limited in the private sector.
As on 31 March 2011, the State had distribution
network of two lakh CKM, 549 sub-stations and
7,600.33 MVA distribution transformers (DTR)
of various categories. There were 105.72 lakh
consumers as of March 2011. The turnover of
the State distribution companies was
` 17,084.67 crore in 2010-11, which represents
3.71 per cent of State Gross Domestic Product.
These companies employed 31,430 employees as
on 31 March 2011.
Distribution network planning
The increase in Company’s distribution capacity
did not match the pace of growth in consumer
demand since connected load grew at 48 per cent
while transformer capacity increased at 27 per
cent during 2006-11. The gap of transformation
capacity to total connected load ranged between
0.63 and 0.82 resulting in frequent tripping and
adverse voltage regulation with consequential
higher quantum of energy losses.
Implementation of Centrally sponsored schemes
Under RGGVY, 3,665 villages were electrified
out of 4,283 villages taken up, while only
12.75 lakh out of 26 lakh BPL households were
provided electric connection during 2006-11.
The Company incurred extra expenditure of
` 102.08 crore in execution of works due to
placement of orders at higher rates compared to
approved estimate, inclusion of price variation
clause instead of fixed cost envisaged in the
scheme and double payment on earthing
materials. Besides, Company had to forego
administrative charges of
` 66.08 crore as
estimates exceeded sanction limits.
Implementation of Restructured Accelerated
Power Development Reforms Programme
(RAPDRP), intended to str engthen Distribution
Management System and upgradation of sub-
transmission & distribution network, fell short
of target and the Company utilised 24 per cent
of the funds released due to delay in completing
loan formalities and slow progress of work.
Operational efficiency
The power purchases from State and Central
PSUs were not adequate to fulfill the demand in
the State and shortfall was met through
purchases from IPPs and other sources at
higher rates ranging from
` 2.49 per unit to
` 4.30 per unit. The energy losses of
3,396 MUs valuing ` 1,311.47 crore were in
excess of norms approved by WBERC. The
main reasons for such losses were inadequate
transformation capacity, high interruption, non
rationalisation of feeders, low power factor, low
feeder availability, theft of electricity, etc. The
Company delayed in rationalising feeders that
led to non reduction of line loss of 865.24 MUs
valued
` 269.96 crore. Further, there was
significant shortfall in addition of capacitor
banks which led to loss of targeted energy
saving of 73.60 MUs valued at
` 22.96 crore.
The percentage of consumers checked was
negligible in all the years and the unrealised
amounts were on the rise.
Financial management
The Company’s Accumulated Losses decreased by
45 per cent between 2007-08 to 2010-11 as they had
earned profit of
` 305.25 crore. In this period,
Annual Revenue Requirement petitions were filed
on time. However, the percentage of deficit in
recovery of fixed cost varied from 8 to 38 per cent
during 2007-11. Besides, as of March 2011 the
Company had retained Regulatory Assets
aggregating to
` 3,320.05 crore. Agriculture was
heavily subsidised with only 31 to 50 per cent of
cost of supply being recovered. Commercial
consumers bore this burden.

Billing efficiency
Energy billed during 2007-11 rose from 73.47
to 79.80 per cent of the total energy available
for sale. This increase was due to installation
of electronic meters which led to accurate
billing. Average billing declined from 4.42 per
cent to 1.13 per cent during this period due to
decline in consumers with defective meters.
Wrong classification of commercial units as
industrial units led to loss of revenue of
` 1.20 crore to the Company. In 15 divisions
during 2008-09 to 2010-11, 21.63 lakh bills
against 5.67 lakh L&MV consumers were short
of minimum charges. Besides, average bills for
86,057 consumers with defective meters could
not be raised since previous meter readings
were not recorded.
Revenue collection efficiency
The outstanding dues from consumers
decreased from
` 1,234.81 crore in 2006-07 to
` 1,047.80 crore in 2010-11. Of the above, dues
of ` 585.51 crore from 15 divisions indicated
that dues outstanding for more than three years
amounted to ` 136.37 crore (23.29 per cent)
while an amount of ` 85.20 crore (14.55 per
cent) was due from disconnected consumers.
Further, arrears of more than rupees one lakh
was due from 3,834 L&MV consumers in
15 divisions and 3,029 HT and EHT consumers
of the Company, for three to 318 months but
their supply was not disconnected resulting in
accumulation of arrears of
` 236.13 crore
(March 2011).
The Company had temporarily disconnected
supply of power to 79 L&MV consumers in
15 divisions and 449 HT and EHT consumers of
the Company, having arrear of more than rupees
one lakh for four to 189 months but were not
permanently disconnected. This resulted in non-
realisation of arrears amounting to
` 22.05 crore
(March 2011). In addition, cheques of
` 3.12 crore had not been credited by the
concerned banks in six divisions but the
Company could not identify the consumers.
Consumer satisfaction
The Company created (January 2009)
Customer Relation Management (CRM) Cell to
look into the grievances of consumers and their
redressal. The Company paid
` 3.26 crore as
compensation to the consumers for
non-compliance of WBERC Regulations.
Energy Conservation
The Company is State Designated Agency
(SDA) under the Energy Conservation
Act, 2001 (Act). BEE had disbursed
(January 2008 to April 2011)
` 1.95 crore to the
Company for energy conservation. The Act
stipulates that the State Government was to
constitute Energy Conservation Fund for
promotion of efficient use of energy and its
conservation. The State Government belatedly
(September 2010) notified creation of West
Bengal Conservation Fund. They are yet to
contribute their share to the fund.
Energy accounting and audit
The Company placed (October 2006/
April 2007) orders on Secure Meters Limited
(SML) for erection of 15,230 energy accounting
meters at an extra expenditure of
` 2.43 crore
towards higher erection charges and payment
of service tax included in the rates. Further,
the Company incurred extra expenditure of
` 10.15 crore by allowing maintenance charges
on these meters though the purchase orders
provided for maintenance of these meters free
of cost for five years.
Due to erroneous stock accounting, the
Company procured 4.42 lakh meters worth
` 40.58 crore in excess of requirement.
Besides, we could not vouchsafe existence of
1.40 lakh meters valued ` 13.17 crore.
Conclusion and Recommendations
The Company did not prepare target for annual
capacity development of sub-stations over the
review period. The increase in distribution
capacity did not match the pace of growth in
consumer demand. They incurred extra
expenditure on execution of rural
electrification work on placement of orders at
higher rates. High energy losses were due to
low feeder availability, high interruption,
voltage fluctuation, inadequate number of
shunt capacitors and low power factor. The
Company lost opportunity to earn higher
revenue due to incorrect application of tariff,
under assessment of revenue and short levy of
minimum charges. The review contains six
recommendations which include creation of
infrastructural facilities keeping in view
demand growth, reduction of high energy losses
by installing adequate number of shunt
capacitors, minimising interruptions and
voltage fluctuations. Achieving 100 per cent
energy billing, applying correct tariffs and
levying minimum applicable consumer charges
as well as optimising internal resource
generation by improving billing and collection
efficiency and vigorously pursuing
outstanding dues.

Introduction
2.1.1 Electricity is an essential requirement for all facets of our life. It has
been recognized as a basic human need. It is a critical infrastructure on which
the socio-economic development of the country depends. Supply of electricity
at reasonable rate to rural India is essential for its overall development. Equally
important is availability of reliable and quality power at competitive rates to
Indian industry to make it globally competitive and to enable it to exploit the
tremendous potential of employment generation. Service sector has made
significant contribution to the growth of our economy. Availability of quality
supply of electricity is very crucial to sustained growth of this segment.
Recognising that electricity is one of the key drivers for rapid economic
growth and poverty alleviation, the natio n has set itself the target of providing
access to all households in next five years.
Major responsibility for achieving the key parameters of the above said
importance of electricity devolves on t he distribution sector. Distribution
sector is very near to people. Distribu tion Companies (DISCOMs) are first
point of contact in the electricity sector for millions of Indians. This is the
sector, which provides electricity to the doorstep of every household. It serves
various objectives of electricity sector such as access to electricity for all
households, supply of reliable and quality power of specified standards in an
efficient manner and at reasonable r ates and at the same time protects the
consumer interest. To achieve the above objectives, DISCOMs need to make
a financial turnaround and they should be commercially viable.
In this review, it is proposed to analyse how far the West Bengal State
Electricity Distribution Company Limited (Company) planned their operations
to achieve above objectives, their fi nancial turnaround and the problems
encountered during the five year period from 2006-07 to 2010-11.
